story:
This sycamore holds a crown 30 metres wide on a trunk only 2.42 metres round, and the Forest Preserves of Cook County rank it third among the sycamores on their land. They measured it on 7 December 2023 at 34.1 metres tall, 112 feet, with the crown about 30.5 metres one way and 24 the other.

Set it beside the county champion at Riverside Lawn, also on this page, and the two look like different ideas of the same tree. The champion is 41.5 metres tall on a trunk 3.91 metres round. This one gives up seven metres of height and a metre and a half of girth, and still spreads nearly as wide. Further north, the state champion sycamore of Wisconsin in downtown Fond du Lac is 6.48 metres round, well over twice this trunk.

It stands in McClaughrey Springs Woods, about half a kilometre from the second-ranked white oak there, which is heavier in the trunk than the county's champion white oak. The black walnut with the widest crown on this page is about 1.5 kilometres away in Swallow Cliff Woods, so the three make a good morning in the south-west preserves.

The register is the only source and gives no age. A visitor recorded a tree beside it in October 2026, which suggests, but does not prove, that this one is still standing. If you know how old it is, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its crown, about 30 metres across, on a slim trunk 2.42 metres round and 34.1 metres tall. It stands at the register's point in McClaughrey Springs Woods.
name: The Third-Ranked Sycamore of McClaughrey Springs Woods

story:
The second-best black cherry in Cook County is 5.4 metres taller than the best. The Forest Preserves of Cook County measured this one in Swallow Cliff Woods on 24 July 2023 at 34.7 metres, 114 feet, which makes it the tallest black cherry on our map. Their champion at Camp Ground Road Woods stops at 29.3 metres, and Wisconsin's state champion, by the Kettle Moraine forest headquarters, at 32.

It loses on the trunk. This one is 2.41 metres round; the champion is 3.35, almost a metre more. The county scores a tree by adding its girth in inches, its height in feet and a quarter of its crown, and those 37 inches of trunk outweigh 18 feet of height. This cherry's crown is slim as well, about 13 metres one way and under 9 the other, so it reads as a tall, narrow tree rather than a broad one.

Swallow Cliff Woods holds more of this page. The second-ranked black walnut, whose crown is the widest here, stands about half a kilometre away, and the county's champion shagbark hickory is in the same preserve.

The register is the only source, and it gives no age. We found no recent photograph, but the register's measurement is from 2023 and the record was updated in December 2025.

story:
This white pine has a thicker trunk than the county's champion and is almost ten metres shorter. The Forest Preserves of Cook County measured it in Swallow Cliff Woods on 1 August 2023 at 2.82 metres round and 19.5 metres tall, 64 feet, and ranked it third among the white pines on their land.

The champion, at Busse Forest North on this page, is 2.63 metres round and 29.3 metres tall. This tree is about 19 centimetres thicker and wider in the crown too, about 20 metres one way and 16 the other against the champion's 16 by 10. It is a squat, broad pine where the champion is a tall, slim one, and the county's scoring, which counts height in feet and girth in inches, rewards the champion's ten metres.

White pine is rare in Cook County, which makes two of them on one page a small event. They are not the biggest of their kind we know. In the Nicolet National Forest in northern Wisconsin, the state register records a white pine 47.9 metres tall, more than twice this one's height.

Swallow Cliff Woods holds more of this page within a short walk. The second-ranked black walnut is about 400 metres away. The register is the only source, and it gives no age; someone recorded a tree nearby in May 2026.
name: The Third-Ranked Eastern White Pine of Swallow Cliff Woods

story:
Cook County ranks this pin oak only third, and it is taller than the champion. The Forest Preserves of Cook County record it in Schiller Woods at 29.3 metres, 96 feet, on a trunk 2.79 metres round, with a crown about 19 metres one way and 16 the other.

All three of the county's top pin oaks are now on this page, and they rank in an order you would not guess by eye. The champion at Rolling Knolls is the shortest of them at 29 metres, but it is 3.59 metres round with a crown about 26 metres across, and the county's score adds trunk, height and crown together. The second, at St. Paul Woods, is the tallest at 31.7. This one sits in between on height and last on girth, which is where it loses. For a pin oak of real bulk, the Wisconsin state champion in Madison's Camp Randall Memorial Park is 3.94 metres round.

In October the leaves turn dark red to russet, the pin oak's best season. Schiller Woods also holds the American elm on this page, about 800 metres away, so the two make a short walk along the preserve.

The register is the only source and gives no age. It also carries no measurement date, though the record was last updated in April 2025, and we found no recent photograph of this tree. If you have seen it, tell us.

story:
The oak Northwestern University's landscape architect chose as her favourite on campus is neither the tallest nor the widest. What it may have is age. In the university's magazine in 2018 she put this bur oak at perhaps 250 years, which would mean it was already growing in the 1770s, and a student nature magazine repeated the figure in 2022.

Her reasoning is in its branches. They grow out horizontally, and she reads that as a sign that it is one of the last survivors of the oak savanna that covered the south end of the campus before the university was built. That is a judgement by someone who has looked after these grounds since 1984, not a ring count, so we keep the age broad, somewhere between 200 and 300 years.

The campus has lost its great trees before. The Old Oak, a white oak near University Hall, died in 1904 at an estimated 500 years or more, by the same magazine's account. If the landscape architect is right, this bur oak is among the last of the trees that were here before the campus.

It stands on the university's grounds just east of 1835 Hinman, a student residence, across Sheridan Road from Fisk Hall in Evanston. Nobody has published its girth or height. The CTA Purple Line and Metra both run to Evanston from the Loop, with stops at Foster and Davis, and from either it is a walk to Sheridan Road.
